awd_titl_txt: Field and radiometric assessments of unexamined fossiliferous caves
awd_abstract_narration:
The fossil record informs evolutionary history, but current knowledge has been drawn from finds located in a small number of sites from geographically restricted areas. This situation partially accounts for existing gaps in the fossil record, limiting knowledge regarding fundamental questions about our species. This study aims to expand the evolutionary record by (i) surveying for new fossil-rich cave sites, (ii) conducting exploratory excavations to evaluate the fossil record preserved within them, and (iii) dating the cave sites to establish the age of the fossiliferous deposits. The project enhances US research capacity by providing student training opportunities and strengthening research links across a broad network of scholars. 

This project examines the paleoanthropological and paleontological research potential of fossiliferous caves through a combination of drone-assisted and pedestrian surveys. At five caves known or suspected to preserve rich fossil deposits, paleontological test excavations document the fossil record preserved within them. Samples generated through excavations are used for radiometric dating, utilizing a combination of radiocarbon and U-series approaches. This project expands paleontological and paleoanthropological research.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Africa’s fossil sites from the last ~6,000,000 years preserve a longer record of human evolution and its ecological context than anywhere else on Earth. These sites document major evolutionary milestones within the human lineage, with the associated mammalian fossil record providing insights into the ecological forces that shaped human evolution. However, despite the enormous size of Africa, its fossil record relevant to human evolution derives primarily from a few small windows across the continent. As a result, the fossil record of human evolution is incomplete, lacking data from many regions and time periods, and posing a major obstacle for addressing fundamental questions in human origins research. A solution to this limitation is to expand the fossil record through investigation of new sites. With support from this High-Risk Research in Biological Anthropology and Archaeology (HRRBAA) award, our team conducted exploratory research aiming to evaluate the paleontological potential of poorly documented caves in South Africa’s Cango Valley, a region far from many of the well-known fossil sites that have illuminated our deep evolutionary past. This entailed survey and exploration of new caves, preliminary test excavations, and dating of geological samples. In doing so, our work provided field and lab-based training opportunities for US and South African students as part of a collaborative international research program.

 

Intellectual Merit: This exploratory, high-risk research was remarkably successful. First, with support from the local community, we gained access to properties that were previously unexplored, identifying several undocumented caves with high paleontological research potential. Second, text excavation and fossil collection at four caves identified during previous surveys generated well-preserved large mammal fossil collections. Subsequent analysis of the fossils demonstrated an exceptional diversity of extant and extinct large mammal species that collectively suggest an age range of ~780,000 to 12,000 years ago. This included recovery of a well-preserved cranium belonging to a new species of fossil antelope. Third, we were able to constrain the ages of the fossil deposits from three of the four caves through radiometric dating of flowstones—mineral deposits formed through flowing water. Consistent with the fossil evidence, these age estimates range from ~20,000 years ago to >500,000 years ago, attesting to a lengthy fossil sequence that encompasses the origin of Homo sapiens and considerably extends the temporal extent of the regional fossil record. Collectively, our ongoing work suggests that the Cango Valley has significant potential to expand our understanding of human and mammal community evolution, setting the stage for decades of future work. We anticipate several publications arising from this research, including a broad overview of the Cango Valley caves, a detailed report describing the fossil vertebrates, and a separate paper describing the new species of fossil antelope.

 

Broader impacts: Our work provided field, laboratory, and research training opportunities for one postdoc and four graduate student collaborators from the US and South Africa. Student collaborators were involved in fieldwork, analysis of the fossil vertebrate remains, and the dating of geological samples as part of an international research team, developing skills and forging connections that will shape their ongoing professional development. In addition, our work strengthened connections across scientists from seven institutions and four countries. Our project moved beyond the ‘helicopter science’ model that is common in paleoanthropology, in that it involves meaningful collaboration with local scientists, with a project leadership team that included an even balance of US and South African nationals. Lastly, our research was highlighted at several public outreach events at the Natural History Museum of Utah, an institution that receives ~300,000 visitors annually.
